request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 46-year-old male

Admission date: [DATE]

Discharge date: [DATE]

Medical history: None reported except exertional dyspnea.

Chief complaint: Exertional dyspnea

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a chief complaint of exertional dyspnea. Physical examination revealed a systolic mitral murmur and a diastolic aortic murmur. TTE revealed a noncoronary SVA protruding into the mitral anterior leaflet, leading to moderate mitral regurgitation, severe aortic insufficiency, and a dilated aortic root. The ascending aorta measured 54-mm, and the left ventricular diastolic diameter was 75-mm, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 66%. No ventricular septal defect was detected. Coronary CTA showed no abnormalities or stenoses found in the coronary tree and the sac of the noncoronary SVA (measuring 36 × 47 × 51 mm) was protruding into the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. Surgery was performed via median sternotomy. The thickening of the wall of the tricuspid aortic valve and ascending aortic wall was consistent with inflammation. The patient underwent mitral valve and aortic valve replacement and replacement of the ascending aorta with an artificial vessel. Antibiotics were administered for 5 weeks. Follow-up TTE showed satisfactory functioning of both replaced valves. Aortic CTA demonstrated restoration of the normal anatomical relationship at the aortic root. The patient was discharged in stable condition.
Discharge diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge instructions: The patient was advised to follow-up with a primary care physician and cardiologist and adhere to medication and lifestyle modification recommendations.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The main condition is a noncoronary sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (SVA). It protrudes into the mitral anterior leaflet and causes severe aortic insufficiency, moderate mitral regurgitation and a dilated aortic root. The surgical findings of inflammation, together with 5 weeks of antibiotics, suggest an infective or inflammatory cause such as syphilitic or infectious aortitis. Whether the SVA is congenital or acquired is not stated.

Candidate codes:
- Q25.4 (congenital malformation of the aorta, other) would apply to a congenital sinus of Valsalva aneurysm.
- I71.x covers aortic aneurysm. An aneurysm of the sinus of Valsalva that is not ruptured would be coded I71.2 or I71.4, and the ascending aorta aneurysm is also I71.
- I35.x covers nonrheumatic aortic valve disorders. Severe aortic insufficiency belongs here (I35.1).
- I08 covers multiple valve disease, but the cause is not rheumatic.

The patient was admitted for exertional dyspnea, and the surgery addressed the SVA, the aortic root and the ascending aorta, with the valve replacements done as part of the repair. The aneurysm is the underlying condition driving the episode. A noncoronary SVA in a 46-year-old with no other history is most often congenital, which would point to Q25. However, the ascending aorta dilation of 54 mm and the inflammatory wall thickening suggest an acquired aortic aneurysm, so I71 is the better fit. The antibiotics suggest an infective process, but the diagnosis is not clearly identified. I will choose I71.

CODE: I71
